title: Game 8: Hans vs Magnus
notes: Game 8 of 12 in the experiment, from the French Defence. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

This is the Classical French; I considered 4.Bg5 and 4.e5, and chose the Steinitz 4.e5, which gains space and kicks the knight to d7 where it is passive. After 4...Nfd7 I plan 5.f4 and 6.Nf3 with a strong central grip, and there are no tactical issues since nothing of mine is loose.

This is the Steinitz French; 4...Ne4 just loses a piece to Nxe4 and the other retreats (Ng8/Nh5/Ng4) are bad, so I play the main line 4...Nfd7, keeping the knight supported and preparing ...c5 to hit d4 before White consolidates.

This is the French Steinitz variation, and the main line reinforces the e5 wedge so that Black's ...c5 can be met with Nf3 and strong central pressure. I checked Nxd5 but after exd5 I'm just a piece down for a pawn, so f4 is the principled choice.

This is the French Steinitz; White's f4 leaves d4 under-defended, so the thematic 5...c5 strikes the base of the pawn chain at once — my notebook's "delay the break" rule concerns premature breaks, while here c5 is the standard, well-supported counterattack. I checked White's replies: 6.dxc5 Nc6 regains the pawn, 6.Nf3 Nc6 keeps pressure, and Bb5 is no check since my knight sits on d7, so no tactic hits me.

This is the French Steinitz with 5.f4, where the main line is to develop and support the d4/e5 wedge; 6.Nf3 brings the knight out and makes cxd4 harmless since Nxd4 keeps a strong grip on the dark squares. I avoided dxc5 (releasing the tension too early) and Nxd5, which loses a piece to exd5.

This is the French Advance/Steinitz structure, where the main line is to pile up on d4 rather than release the tension: 6...Nc6 develops a piece, keeps the c5/Nc6 pressure on d4, and avoids 6...cxd4 7.Nxd4 which hands White a free developing recapture. I checked White's forcing tries — 7.dxc5 Bxc5 is comfortable for me, and the tempting 6...Qh4+ 7.g3 just loses time with my queen, while 6...Nxe5 7.dxe5 drops a piece for a pawn chain.

Black's last move piles up on d4, so I need to shore up the center; Be3 develops a piece while defending d4, and if Black trades with cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 Bxd4 I keep a strong centralized bishop and space advantage. I rejected dxc5 since Bxc5 gives Black easy play and releases the central tension too early, and Nxd5 simply loses a pawn to exd5.

This is the French Steinitz; the main line is to release the tension with 7...cxd4 so that after 8.Nxd4 I can hit the knight with ...Bc5 and develop with tempo. I checked 7...Nxd4 8.Nxd4 cxd4 9.Bxd4 — material is level but it hands White an ideal centralised bishop, and 7...Qb6 8.Na4 just chases my queen, so the recapture chain favours cxd4.

Black has just taken on d4 in the Steinitz French, and I want to recapture with the knight to keep my strong e5/f4 pawn structure and good piece activity. 8.Nxd4 is the main line; after 8...Nxd4 9.Bxd4 or 8...Bc5 9.Qd2 I'm comfortably developed, whereas Qxd4 or Bxd4 would invite ...Nxe5 tricks or loose piece placement.

This is the main-line French Steinitz, where 8...Bc5 is the natural developing move: it pressures the d4 knight and trades off White's good dark-squared bishop, and I checked the recapture chains — 9.Nxc6 bxc6 10.Bxc5 Nxc5 and 9.Ncxd5 exd5 10.Nxc6 bxc6 both leave me fine or a piece up. White has no checks or captures (Nxe6 fails to fxe6), and unlike my old ...Bb6 error this bishop is active rather than passive.

Both my d4-knight and e3-bishop are under pressure from Black's Bc5 and Nc6, so I want to add support and develop; 9.Qd2 defends the bishop, keeps the knight chain intact, and prepares queenside castling. Tactical shots like Nxe6 or Nxd5 just lose a piece, and after 9...Bxd4 10.Bxd4 Nxd4 11.Qxd4 I keep a pleasant space advantage.

Counting the full chain on d4, 9...Bxd4 10.Bxd4 Nxd4 11.Qxd4 is a clean even trade (bishop+knight each way), and 11.Nxd5 exd5 12.Qxd4 would just lose a piece for White. I avoid 9...Nxd4 because 10.Bxc5! leaves my knight on d4 hanging to Qd2 with no comfortable defence, so the bishop must capture first.

Black has traded off my strong d4 knight, so I simply recapture with the bishop, keeping my queen active and preserving the e5 space advantage. After 10...Nxd4 11. Qxd4 Qb6 12. Qd2 I keep a pleasant space edge with Black's light-squared bishop still passive, whereas recapturing with the queen immediately invites tempo-gaining knight moves.

I first checked the a7-g1 diagonal and saw that both 10...Qb6 and 10...Nc5 simply lose material to Bxb6/Bxc5, and 10...Ncxe5 11.fxe5 Nxe5 12.Bxe5 drops a piece for two pawns. So I trade off White's powerful dark-squared bishop: after 10...Nxd4 11.Qxd4 nothing of mine hangs (a7 is covered by the rook, d5 by e6 and my queen), and I can follow with ...Qb6 to offer a queen trade and equalise.

Black's knight on d4 is simply hanging, so I can recapture; I checked 11.Nxd5 but then 11...Nxc2+ 12.Qxc2 Nb6 13.Nxb6 Qxb6 gives Black activity against b2 and equal material, so the greedy line wins nothing. Instead Qxd4 recaptures while centralizing the queen, keeping my strong e5/f4 space, the knight on c3, and no counterplay for Black — I'll follow with Bd3 and castling.

Nxe5 loses a piece since Qd4 guards e5, and Qh4+ is just met by 12.g3 with tempo gain for White. Instead I challenge White's dominant centralized queen with 11...Qb6: b2 is undefended (Ra1 doesn't cover it), Bb5+ is impossible because my knight on d7 blocks that diagonal, and after Qxb6 Nxb6 I get a comfortable structure with Bd7 and castling to follow.

Black's Qb6 both attacks my undefended Qd4 (along the b6–d4 diagonal) and the loose b2 pawn, and every attempt to hold on (Rd1, Ne2, Na4) drops a pawn or runs into Qa5+ winning a piece. Nxd5 only nets two pawns for the knight, so the clean solution is to trade queens, after which I keep my space advantage with e5/f4 against Black's passive light-squared bishop in a level endgame.

I must recapture the queen on b6, and I prefer the knight so my pawn structure stays healthy (a7/b7 intact) instead of doubling pawns with axb6. I checked White's follow-ups: 13.Bb5+ is met by 13...Bd7 or Nd7, and 13.Nb5 threatening Nc7+ (forking king and rook) is answered by 13...Kd8 or Rb8, after which the knight on b6 heads for c4.

Nxd5 just loses a piece to Nxd5 or exd5, and Bb5+ would trade off Black's bad light-squared bishop, which helps him; instead I develop with Bd3, keeping the strong e5 wedge and preparing O-O plus Ne2–d4 or f5 pressure. If Black tries Nc4, Bxc4 dxc4 leaves him with a weak isolated pawn while my space advantage remains.

Material is equal with queens off, and my only real problem is the undeveloped kingside and the passive c8 bishop, so following my rule about castling before any central or wing action, I bring the king to safety; Bxh7+ is harmless since Kxh7 just wins the bishop, and after a future f5 exf5 Bxf5 Bxf5 Rxf5 I stand fine with ...Nc4 hitting b2. Tempting ...Nc4 immediately only invites b3 kicking the knight back, so castling is the solid choice.

Bxh7+ fails since there's no Ng5+ follow-up, and Nxd5 just loses a piece to exd5, so I'll develop sensibly. Castling long connects my rooks, puts a rook on the d-file against Black's d5 pawn, and keeps my king away from the kingside where I want to expand with g4 and f5 against the e6/d5 chain.

Queens are off and my main problem is the blocked light-squared bishop behind d5/e6, so I want the classic French freeing break; 14...f6 15.exf6 Rxf6 opens the f-file, gives my rook activity and prepares ...e5 or ...Bd7 to free the bishop. I checked White's replies: there are no checks or loose-piece hits (Bxh7+ is harmless with queens gone, g7 stays guarded by the king), whereas 14...Nc4 15.Bxc4 dxc4 would leave me a weak c4 pawn on an open file and trade off White's good bishop for my knight.

Nxd5 just drops a piece (Nxd5 Nxd5 Rxd5 exd5) and f5 fails to exf5 since Bxf5 loses the bishop to Bxf5, while exf6 Rxf6 leaves my f4 pawn loose on an open file. So I'll develop with Rhe1, which supports the cramping e5 wedge, keeps Nc3 eyeing d5, and after ...fxe5 fxe5 leaves Black with a backward e6 pawn on a half-open file.

My worst piece is the c8 bishop, so I develop it with ...Bd7, keeping the f6/e5 tension and preparing ...Be8/...Bb5 or ...Rae8. I checked the only tactic, 16.Nxd5, and it fails to 16...Nxd5! 17.Bxd5 exd5, netting me a piece for a pawn; 16.f5 exf5 and 16.Bxh7+ Kxh7 simply drop material, and d7 can't be attacked since the d-file is blocked by my own pawn.

Bxh7+ just drops a bishop (Kxh7 with no follow-up), and Nxd5 fails because after exd5 the recapture on d5 is covered by the knight on b6 — I end up a pawn down on the exchanges. Instead I'll reroute with Ne2 heading for d4, where the knight hits e6, blockades the d-pawn and keeps my cramping e5 wedge intact.

I first checked the tempting ...Nc4 and ...Bb5 and rejected both on the recapture chain — after ...Nc4 Bxc4 dxc4 the d-file opens and Rxd7 wins my undefended bishop, and ...Bb5 is simply Bxb5 with nothing to recapture; ...d4 drops to Rxd4 as well. So I resolve the centre with ...fxe5: White must answer fxe5 (my new e5 pawn hits f4), after which his e5 pawn is permanently blocked by my e6, my rook already sits on the open f-file, and I saw no check or capture (Bxh7+ just loses to Kxh7) that wins anything.

Bxh7+ just loses a piece after Kxh7, so I simply recapture with fxe5, keeping material equal and gaining a space-gaining passed-ish pawn on e5 that cramps Black's position. If Black tries Rf2 to raid, I have Nd4 hitting e6 with enough counterplay (Rxg2 Nxe6) to stay level.

White's Bd3 is his most dangerous piece (it also guards f5, so ...Rf5 loses a rook to Bxf5), so I offer to trade it off with ...Nc4, where the knight is attacked once by the bishop and defended once by my d5 pawn — Bxc4 dxc4 is an even trade that leaves me the bishop in an open position. Note b2 is not really loose since Kc1 guards it (…Nxb2 Kxb2), and if White kicks with b3 I retreat to the good square d6 rather than leaving the knight unsupported.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 18. Bxc4 Rf2 19. g4 Rxh2 20. Bd3 Rf8

moves.thought: My e5 pawn and b2 are both hit by the knight on c4, and no quiet move defends e5 (Ne2 blocks my rook), so I eliminate the annoying knight. After Bxc4 dxc4 Black is left with a weak c4 pawn and a backward e6 pawn, and my rooks plus knight (Nd4/Rd4) can pressure both.

The obvious 18...dxc4 opens the d-file and my bishop on d7 is completely undefended, so 19.Rxd7 just wins it back — I checked the whole chain and there's no counter-resource. Instead 18...Rad8 defends d7 and renews the threat of ...dxc4, forcing White's loose bishop (attacked by d5, defended by nothing) to move; if White grabs with 19.Bxd5 exd5 20.Rxd5 I have 20...Bc6 hitting the rook and only drop pawns rather than a piece, and my f8 rook stays on the open file.

I can't win the d5 pawn by force (Bxd5 exd5 Rxd5 Rxd5 just drops a rook), so I want to add pressure instead: Nf4 hits both d5 and e6, and if Black pushes ...d4 then Nxe6 or Bxe6+ wins a pawn cleanly. If Black answers ...Rf5 to harass the knight, I simply play g3 defending it with the follow-up g4 gaining time on the rook.

I'm currently a piece down because 18...Rad8 ignored the capture on c4, so recovering material is urgent: Bc4 is completely undefended and my d5 pawn can take it. I checked the follow-up 20.Nxe6 "fork" of my rooks — my bishop on d7 guards e6, so 20...Bxe6 simply nets a knight, and 20.Rxd7 Rxd7 only gives up rook for bishop; after dxc4 material is level with my bishop against his knight.

review.label: mistake
review.refutation: 20. Rd4 b5 21. h4 Bc8 22. Rxd8 Rxd8

moves.thought: Rd4 looks tempting against the loose c4 pawn but drops a rook to Rxd8-d4, so instead Re4 hits c4 along the fourth rank while still guarding my e5 pawn and keeping Rd1 pressing the pinned-ish Bd7. Nxe6 fails simply to Bxe6 since my own e5 pawn blocks the e-file recapture, so I build pressure: after ...b5 I can undermine with a4, and after ...Bc6 I just take with Rxc4, hitting the bishop.

The c4 pawn is attacked by Re4, but my e6 pawn is attacked by Nf4 and defended only by Bd7 — so every bishop move (Bb5, Bc6) runs into Nxe6! forking both rooks, which loses a rook for a knight. Rxf4 also loses a rook since Re4 guards f4, so instead I defend c4 with the rook while keeping Bd7 on guard duty for e6; after 21.Nxe6 Bxe6 22.Rxe6 Rxc2+ 23.Kb1 Rxg2 I'm even a pawn up.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 21. Rxd7 Rc6 22. Red4 h6 23. g3 c3

moves.thought: Black's e6 pawn is only defended by the bishop, and my Re4 backs up the knight, so Nxe6 Bxe6 Rxe6 wins a clean pawn while leaving me a strong e5 passer. Importantly, Black's own c4 pawn blocks the c8-rook, so there's no counterplay with ...Rxc2+ after the exchanges; if Black declines with ...Rfe8, Nxg7 picks up a second pawn.

White's Ne6 forks my f8 rook and g7, so any move like Rc6/Rce8 loses the exchange to Nxf8; counting the chain, Bxe6 Rxe6 is a clean bishop-for-knight trade that eliminates White's most active piece and leaves me only a pawn down with two rooks each. Kf7 also defends f8, but then the knight retreats to d4 with tempo and my loose c4 pawn plus White's active rooks give him a free hand, so I take the knight now.

I'm down a bishop for a pawn, so I need activity — note that the bishop on e6 covers c4, d5 and d7, so Rxc4, Rd5 and Rd7 all just drop material. Rd6 is safe (nothing covers d6), hits the undefended bishop with tempo, and if Black tries Bd5 I win it with Rxd5 since both rooks would hit it; after a retreat like Bf5 I can swing to b6 against b7.

My bishop on e6 is attacked by Rd6 and undefended, so I must move it; Bd7/Bd5 drop to Rxd7/Rxd5 and Bh3 to gxh3, while Bf5 saves it with tempo by hitting the loose Re4 and also eyeing c2. If White tries 23.Rf4 to harass it, 23...Bg6 leaves that rook hanging on the f-file, and after Rxf8+ Kxf8 my Rc8 still guards c4, keeping me a clean bishop for a pawn up.

My rook on e4 is attacked by the bishop on f5, so it must move or trade — and Rxc4 lets it grab a pawn on the way. After Rxc4 Rxc4 I'm down only a bishop for two pawns in a single-rook endgame, where my passed e-pawn and 3-v-2 queenside majority give real counterplay, far better than passively retreating and staying two points down.

White's rook just landed on c4 and it is completely undefended — c2 and b2 pawns cannot recapture, and nothing else guards the square — while my c8 rook attacks it down the open c-file (c5, c6, c7 all empty). After 23...Rxc4 White's only ideas are 24.Rd8 (not a check, and f8 is defended by my king) or 24.Rd7, both met easily, leaving me a full rook and bishop ahead.

I'm down a lot of material, so I need a safe, active square — note the bishop on f5 covers d7, e6 and d3, so Rd7/Re6/Rd3 all drop the rook, and Rd4 (Rxd4) or e6 (Rc6!) also lose material. Rd5 is untouchable, defends my e5 pawn, and pins the bishop to its defender: if the f8 rook ever leaves the f-file, Rxf5 wins the bishop.

Rd5 only covers the d-file and a5/b5/c5, so trade offers like Rc5 or Rd4 would just drop a rook for free, and Be6/Bd7/Bxc2 lose the bishop (c2 is guarded by the king). Be4 instead attacks the rook from a square my c4-rook defends, so White must retreat (or allow Rxe4 after Rxe4, trading into a hopeless ending) while I keep my rook-and-bishop advantage and aim at e5 and g2.

I'm down a rook and bishop, and Black is threatening both ...Rxc2+ (my king can't recapture because the e4 bishop covers c2) and ...Bxg2. Rd2 is the only move that defends c2 and g2 at once, and if Black tries ...Rxc2+ then Rxc2 Bxc2 Kxc2 actually wins material back for me.

I'm up a rook and bishop, so the first priority is safety and simplification, but g2 is completely undefended (the king is on c1), so Bxg2 grabs a free pawn without allowing any tactic — after 26.Rd7 I simply answer Rf7, offering the rook trade with my king defending f7 (Rc7 would lose a rook to Rxc7). Nothing of mine becomes loose: c4 rook and g2 bishop are untouchable by White's lone rook.

Black's bishop just grabbed g2 and is undefended, so my rook on d2 simply takes it — nothing hangs afterwards since c2 is guarded by my king, and Rxc2+ would just lose a rook for a pawn. I'm already down material from the earlier exchange on c4, so winning the bishop back is clearly essential.

I'm a full rook up (two rooks and four pawns vs rook and five pawns), so I just need to mop up safely — Rxc2+ is a trap since Kxc2 recaptures and throws away a rook for one pawn. Re4 attacks the undefended e5 pawn, invites the rook trade Rg4 (which I happily accept when ahead), and if White pushes e6 I simply take with Rxe6.

I'm down a rook, so I need to keep my only rook active and hold the e5 pawn rather than allow trades (Rg4 or Re2 just swaps into a hopeless pawn ending). Rg5 defends e5 along the fifth rank, eyes g7, and if Black tries 27...Rf5 then 28.Rxf5 wins a rook since f5 would cover e5.

I'm actually up a full rook (two rooks vs one), so the key is not to throw it away — Rxe5?? loses a rook because White's Rg5 guards e5 along the fifth rank. Instead 27...Rf5 offers a trade backed by my f8 rook: after 28.Rxf5 Rxf5 my rook also picks up the undefended e5 pawn, and if White declines by moving the rook off the fifth rank I simply take e5 for free.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 28. Rxf5 g6 29. Rf2 Rxe5 30. c4 Re4

moves.thought: Black's rook on f5 is completely undefended — the rook on e4 covers the e-file and the fourth rank but not f5, and the king is too far away. Rxg7+ would just lose my rook to Kxg7, so I simply capture, restoring material balance with an extra pawn in the rook endgame.

White's e5 pawn is passed and his rook on f5 is its only defender, so Rxe5 forces an even trade (Rxe5 Rxe5) that kills the dangerous passer and leaves four pawns each in a drawable pawn endgame; alternatives like Re2 fail to Rh5, which defends both h2 and e5, and Re1+ Kd2 followed by grabbing a2 loses to e6-e7 with Rf8+.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 29. Rxe5 Kf7 30. Rc5 Ke6 31. Rb5 b6

moves.thought: Trading rooks with Rxe5 leads to a dead-drawn symmetrical pawn ending, so instead I invade with Rf7, hitting both b7 and g7 — Black can't offer a trade with Re7 since that square is undefended. After something like Re1+ Kd2 Rh1 Rxg7+ Kf8 Rxh7 Rxh2+, I emerge with a healthy 3-vs-2 queenside majority and real winning chances.

White's 29.Rf7 leaves the rook completely undefended — no white piece or pawn covers f7 (king is on c1, pawns on a2/b2/c2/h2), so Kxf7 simply wins a whole rook, leaving me a rook and four pawns against four pawns. I counted the recapture chain and there is none, and my king on f7 is not attacked by anything.

I'm a full rook down, so my only practical hope is maximum king activity and creating a passed pawn on the queenside; passive pawn moves just let Black's king and rook dominate. Kd2 heads for the center, keeps my pawns flexible, and doesn't walk into any rook check that gains material.

I'm a whole rook up, so the only danger is dropping the rook — Re1, Re2+ and Re3 are all on squares my opponent's king on d2 attacks, so they lose the rook outright (exactly the Kx-capture blunder my rule 12 warns about). Instead I centralize my king with Ke6, keeping the rook safe on e5 where it cuts along the fifth rank, and I'll then march the king to d5/e4 and escort my pawns.

I'm a full rook down, so my only practical hope is king activity and pushing my queenside majority while the h-pawn holds. Centralizing with Kd3 keeps the king in front of the pawns; if Black plays Rd5+ I simply step to c3 or e3 and keep my pawn chain intact, whereas a hasty pawn push would just leave targets for the rook.

I'm a whole rook up, so I just need safe, simple technique: Re2/Re3+ would be snapped off by the king on d3 (rule 12), so I avoid those squares. Ra5 hits the undefended a2 pawn from a safe square, and after winning it my rook sits behind White's queenside pawns while my own pawns stay connected.

I'm a rook down for a pawn, so my only practical chance is to make a compact, mutually defensible pawn mass that my king can shepherd while gaining space. c4 grabs squares, keeps the king on d3 close to the pawns, and after a reply like Rc5 I simply answer Kd4 defending the pawn.

I'm a full rook up, and a2 is completely undefended — White's king on d3 doesn't touch it and the b2 pawn only guards a3/c3, so Rxa2 grabs a free pawn with zero risk. That also puts my rook behind White's queenside pawns, so after the trades I'll have connected passers escorted by rook and king, with no enemy passer to worry about.

I'm down a rook for a pawn, so I just need the most resilient setup: Kc3 defends the b2 pawn and keeps my queenside pawn duo intact, whereas moves like b3, b4 or c5 leave pawns loose to the active rook. Black will likely grab h2, but I keep b2+c4 and try to build a passed pawn with my king nearby.

Rxb2 loses the rook outright to Kxb2, so I checked every king capture first; instead I play Ra4, a square the white king cannot reach, which attacks the c4 pawn and ties White down while my king and pawn mass come forward with the extra rook.

I'm down a rook for a pawn, so my only practical chance is to advance the queenside pawns with king support. Kb3 attacks the rook on a4 and wins a tempo while keeping both b2 and c4 covered (nothing is capturable), after which I can follow with c5 and b4 to build a phalanx.

My rook on a4 is attacked by Kb3, and Rxc4, Ra2, Ra3+ and Rb4+ all drop it to the king (rule 12), while any king move simply loses the rook, so I must retreat it to a safe square. Ra1 keeps the rook maximally active behind White's position, ready to swing to c1/d1 against the c4 and b2 pawns while my king walks up via e5-d4; being a whole rook up, this is a simple technical win.

I'm down a rook for a pawn, so I'm looking for the most active practical try rather than a save. Pushing c5 gains space, keeps my king able to support it from b4, and aims to tie Black's rook to the queenside; passive king moves just let Black's extra kingside pawn roll forward unopposed.

I'm a rook and a pawn up, so I just need to neutralize the only loose White asset — the c5 pawn — without putting anything on a square the king touches. Rc1 is safe (b3 doesn't cover c1), blockades/attacks the c-pawn, and after Kb4 I add Kd5 to win it, while c6 simply loses to bxc6.

My c5 pawn is attacked by the rook, so Kb4 is the only way to hold it; if Black tries Rc4+ Kb5 Rxc5+ Kxc5 I win the queenside pawns and reach a decent pawn race. Pushing c6 just loses the pawn to bxc6, and h3/h4 drops c5 at once.

Rxc5 would be a blunder since Kb4 covers c5 (and Rc4+ drops to Kxc4), so instead I bring my king up with Kd5, which attacks the c5 pawn a second time and also defends c5 so that Rxc5 can never be met by Kxc5. After something like Kb5 Rxc5+ or Kb3 Rxc5 I win the last dangerous pawn and keep a trivially winning rook-plus-pawns endgame.

I'm a rook down for a pawn, so the c5 pawn is doomed once Black plays Rb1 or b6; pushing c6 just trades it off and leaves me with nothing, and any king move drops c5 at once. I'll play h4 to gain space on the only side where I might create counterplay while my king still guards c5.

Rxc5 looks like it drops the rook to Kxc5, but c5 is guarded by my king on d5, so that capture is illegal for White — the pawn is simply free. That leaves me a rook and two extra pawns up with a safe, defended rook, and White's h-pawn is easily stopped by the rook later.

I'm down a rook, and my king on b4 can't capture the c5 rook since it's defended by Kd5, so my only real counterplay is the h-pawn. Pushing h5 gains a tempo of advancement and forces Black to spend time stopping it, which is my only practical hope.

I'm a rook and three pawns up, so White's only counterplay is the h-pawn running; ...h6 permanently blocks it on a square my g7 pawn can't be forced to capture, leaving White with a frozen pawn and nothing to do. My rook on c5 is attacked by the king but defended by my king on d5, so it's safe, and after this I can simply bring king and rook to escort my queenside pawns.

I'm a rook down and can't take on c5 since it's defended by the king, so I must retreat; Ka4 and Ka3 push my king to the edge where it gets cut off. Kb3 keeps the king closer to the center and beside my b2 pawn, giving the most resistance.

I'm a rook and two pawns up, so my only duty is to avoid giving the rook away: c2, c3 and c4 are all attacked by the white king on b3, so Rc2/Rc3+/Rc4 would simply lose to Kx. I centralise with Kd4, keeping the rook safe on c5 and preparing to squeeze the white king off the b2 pawn or escort my queenside pawns.

I'm a rook down with no pawn moves available, so I just need the most resilient king square; Kb4 runs into Rb5+ and Ka4 gets boxed in by ...Kc4 with a quick mate on the a-file. Ka2 keeps the b2 pawn defended and retains the most escape squares (a1, a3, b1) after Black's king advances.

I'm a rook and three pawns up; White's h5 pawn is completely undefended and the e8-h5 diagonal/rank is clear, so Rxh5 wins it for free and leaves White only a b2 pawn. The h5 square is not touched by White's king on a2, so this breaks none of my safety rules, and White still has b2-b3/b4 available so there is no stalemate issue.

I'm down a rook for a pawn and the game is strategically lost, so my only practical chance is to run the b-pawn and create a distant passer that costs Black some time. b4 gains a tempo over b3, and my king can defend from a3 if the rook comes to b5.

I'm a rook and three pawns up, so the only thing to watch is White's b-pawn; Rb5 both blockades it and attacks it, and b5 is not covered by the king on a2, so White can only shuffle while I take on b4 next move. That keeps my king safe inside the square of the only passer and simplifies to a trivial win.

I'm lost material-wise, so my only practical try is to keep the b4 pawn defended and stay active. Kb3 guards b4 (Rxb4+ Kxb4 at least trades the rook off for the pawn), whereas any other king move loses the pawn for free.

The tempting Rxb4+ is a trap — the white king on b3 simply answers Kxb4 and I throw away my rook for one pawn, exactly the kind of "square the enemy king attacks" blunder my rule 12 warns about. Instead I keep the rook safe and cut the white king off on the c-file with Rc5, which also still covers b5 so the b-pawn can never advance, after which my king and four pawns win easily.

I'm lost here — Black has a rook and three extra pawns, and b5 just loses to Rxb5+ leaving me facing rook and pawns. Trading my last pawn for the rook with bxc5 at least eliminates the rook and forces Black to win with pawns alone, giving me the longest practical resistance.

White's king on b3 does not cover c5, so Kxc5 safely snaps off the last white pawn and leaves me with four pawns against a bare king. I checked the king's attacked squares (a2-c4) and c5 is not among them, so there is no stalemate or recapture trick.

new_lessons: [middlegame] When offering a trade, name the defender of the target square in the position after your move; a piece never defends the square it is moving to. Example: 27...Rf5 "backed by my f8 rook" — that rook was the mover; 28.Rxf5 won a clean rook

[middlegame] Play every capture chain on a square to its end, recounting attackers and defenders after each trade; move only if the final material count favours you. Example: ...Qc3 "forked" rooks but bxc3 won the queen; 8.a4 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 removed e4's last guard

[middlegame] Before trading a minor piece, play the recapture: if a pawn recapture opens a file or diagonal toward your king, or leaves pawns loose, keep the piece. Example: 17...Nc4 18.Bxc4 dxc4 opened the e-file for Re4 and left c4 hanging, 51%→9%

[endgame] Before trading the last rooks into a pure pawn endgame, count both kings' distances to every pawn and the race in moves; equal pawns lose if their king is faster. Example: 28...Rxe5 29.Rxe5 gave a "drawable" 4v4, but White's central king outpaced mine, 50%→6%

[middlegame] When a rook can invade the enemy second rank hitting loose pawns, prefer that to any equal trade; with both kings exposed, activity beats simplification. Example: Instead of 17...Nc4, 17...Rf2 taking h2 and tying White down was winning

[middlegame] Before any quiet or developing move, list every enemy check; if a check wins a loose piece (Qa5+/Qh4+), choose another move. Example: 11.Bc4?? Qh4+ 12.Bf2 Qxc4: f3 plus uncastled king made the e1-h4 check decisive, 55%→8%

[middlegame] Every move, name your undefended pieces and the entry squares (c2, d3, g4, your 6th/7th rank) an enemy piece can reach; guard the loosest first. Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn gave Black free tempi ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5; a rook then invaded d6-c6

[endgame] When material ahead, trade one-for-one to keep your extra unit, but never trade your last extra piece or a pawn that is your only winning asset. Example: Refusing 31.Rd5 "to keep the exchange" dropped winning chances 94%→61%

[endgame] Never place a piece on a square the enemy king attacks unless you guard it; before every move in won positions check Kx-captures and stalemate. Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 drew a won queen endgame; earlier 58...Rd4 allowed 60.Kxd4

[endgame] With extra material, first cut off the enemy king and seize the seventh rank; push a pawn only when king or rook escorts it. Example: 59...b5 pushed an unescorted pawn instead of Rd5; loose pawns let the enemy king counterattack

[endgame] Keep extra pawns connected and mutually defended; before grabbing material check your king stays inside the square of every enemy passer. Example: 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6; 44...Kxh4 won a rook but f5-f6 plus the h-pawn made two queens

[middlegame] When a bishop pins your knight against king or loose rook, kick the pinner with a3/h3 or Bd2 instead of passively defending with the queen. Example: 12.Qd2 let ...Nc5-e4 pile on; 12.a3 questioned Bb4 at once, 59%→54%

[middlegame] Keep a knight or bishop on an advanced square only if a pawn can support it; retreat before enemy pawns take every square away. Example: Unsupported Ne4 had no safe retreat after e5/d6; Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns

[middlegame] Never push pawns in front of your castled king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; answer a wing storm with a central break. Example: 17.g3 invited fxg3 and Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[opening] Delay the central break (d5/e5) until minors are developed and the king is castled; when two pieces can recapture, use the minor piece, not the queen. Example: 8...d5 exd5 left a backward pawn, 48%→42%; 10...Qxd5? 11.Qxd5 lost a tempo, 45%→38%
